message.content: Although an Leshy, Pebble Spring became immediately fascinated by the mortal settlements when they set foot in a city. They loved the nicely paved ground, the intricate bridges, and above all, they loved houses. The nicely laid out stone walls formed shelters from the weather yet connected the earth with the stories from every family. They decided to learn the craft of housebuilding with the help of a touch of arcane magic from their self-made staff. The first morning, they stood at the edge of the cobblestone road and watched as the carts rolled by, their wheels clicking against the worn stones. Each house they passed seemed to hum with a quiet warmth, as though the walls themselves remembered every song ever sung within. Pebble Spring reached out a careful hand and pressed it against the rough surface of a chimney, feeling the faint vibration of a hearth fire below. The mortar between the bricks was smooth and even, a small marvel that no amount of magic could easily replicate. They spent the entire day sketching the angles of the rooftops in a leather-bound journal, their staff tapping softly against the ground in rhythm. By evening, the sketches had filled three pages, each line drawn with a precision that surprised even the Leshy themselves. The next morning, a gentle rain began to fall, and the cobblestones glistened under the soft gray light. Pebble Spring walked to the highest bridge in the village and looked down at the river winding below the town. The water caught the reflections of every lantern, turning the surface into a shimmering mosaic of gold and amber. They marveled at how the builders had angled each drain so that the rainwater would flow away from the foundations. It was a small thing, yet it spoke of centuries of careful observation and patient work. Back in the workshop they had claimed near the old mill, Pebble Spring arranged their tools with great care. The staff, carved from a fallen branch of an ancient rowan, glowed faintly at the tip with a soft green pulse. They channeled a thread of arcane energy through the wood, and the air around them shimmered briefly like heat rising from summer stone. A single brick, no larger than a child's palm, levitated gently above the workbench and rotated slowly in the still air. The Leshy studied its edges, noting how the kiln had given it a slightly irregular shape, almost perfect but not quite. This small imperfection, they realized, was what made each brick unique and gave every wall its own quiet character. The seasons passed in a blur of growing and fading, and the village prepared for the first real frost. The leaves on the elms turned to a deep copper, and the air carried a crispness that settled into the stone. By the time the Leshy had walked through every corner of the village and observed how the light fell differently on each stone wall, they noticed that the sky above had taken on a **spotty** quality that none of the elder trees had ever described to them before.
